Where it began

Mohammad Asif was born in December 1982 in Machikay, a small farming village near Sheikhupura in Pakistan's Punjab. He grew up in a family that worked the land and bred animals.

An early believer was Mohammad Haroon, his club captain and coach, who spotted his promise early and became a close friend and adviser. Asif played his domestic cricket for sides including Sheikhupura, Sialkot, Quetta, National Bank and Khan Research Labs, and did well enough to be hurried into the Test squad.

The player

Asif played 23 Tests for Pakistan between 2005 and 2010 and took 106 wickets at 24.37, with seven five-wicket innings and a best of 6 for 41. His debut, against Australia in January 2005, brought 18 overs, no wickets and a nine-wicket defeat, which is one way to learn the job.

His next chance came a year later, at home to India, and at Karachi he made it count. His 4 for 78 helped earn a small first-innings lead, and he then bowled Sehwag, Laxman and Tendulkar in the second as Pakistan won. In Sri Lanka soon after he took 11 for 71 in another victory. Against South Africa in 2007 he took 19 wickets, which lifted him to eighth in the Test rankings after only nine Tests, equalling the Pakistan record for the fewest Tests needed, shared with Waqar Younis and Pervez Sajjad. The ICC put him in its World Test XI for 2007, and in 2010 he was ranked the second-best Test bowler in the world, behind Dale Steyn.

What made him special

His gift was movement. From a short approach and a smooth action that hardly changed, he could swing the ball either way, and by working his fingers at release he could make it dart off the seam as well. Batters had no clue from his action which way it would go. Hashim Amla, AB de Villiers and Kevin Pietersen all counted him among the hardest bowlers they faced, and James Anderson credited watching Asif's wobbling seam with helping him learn his own.

The bat was another matter: 141 Test runs at 5.64. He also made five Test ducks in a row, a record he shared with Bob Holland and Ajit Agarkar, which is at least distinguished company.

In England

Leicestershire signed him for the 2006 season, having seen him in a second XI game in 2004, and he took 25 first-class wickets in seven matches before joining Pakistan's tour of England.

And finally

Twenty20 was built for batters, and bowlers in it expect to go for runs. Asif was the first man to bowl a maiden over in the format, and he took two wickets in it as well: Kevin Pietersen first ball, then Andrew Strauss, also for nothing. In a game made for hitting, six balls with nothing to hit is quite a trick.
